story.headline: ICJ rules Myanmar committed genocide
story.summary: The Gambia's genocide case against Myanmar decided by the ICJ.
story.display_body: The International Court of Justice (ICJ) ruled on Thursday 19 November that Myanmar acted with genocidal intent against the Rohingya in its 2017 military campaign, deciding the case The Gambia brought in 2019 under the 1948 Genocide Convention. Reading the judgment over about three hours, Court President Yuji Iwasawa said the evidence showed that Myanmar's security forces killed some 10,000 Rohingya, committed widespread sexual violence and extreme violence against children, and attacked people as they fled to Bangladesh. The court said the "only reasonable inference" from the pattern of atrocities was an intent to destroy a "substantial part" of the group. It also found that Myanmar "violated its obligation to prevent genocide" by letting armed civilians join the campaign. Myanmar had argued that the operation responded to attacks on police posts by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army. The crackdown drove more than 730,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh, and about 1.2 million now live in camps around Cox's Bazar. ICJ judgments are final and cannot be appealed, but the court has no means of enforcing them itself.
story.why: Swiss broadcaster SRF calls it the first time the UN's highest court has found a state responsible for genocide. In 2007, in Bosnia's case against Serbia, the court found only that Serbia had failed to prevent genocide at Srebrenica. The ruling gives the Rohingya a legal finding they can use in claims for return, reparations and prosecutions, and it is a precedent for other genocide cases now before the court.

story.headline: Xi, Trump and Putin meet in Shenzhen
story.summary: First US-China-Russia trilateral leaders' meeting at APEC in Shenzhen.
story.display_body: Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin held their first three-way meeting on Thursday 19 November in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, after Trump met each of them separately. Opening the talks, Xi called the meeting of "groundbreaking significance" and, according to China's Xinhua agency, said nuclear weapons "should be comprehensively banned and thoroughly destroyed". Trump said the three countries were "uniquely positioned" to discuss nuclear weapons; New START, the last US–Russia arms-control treaty, expired this year without a successor. Putin said Ukraine would be the focus of his talks. The closed-door session was short: Al Jazeera, citing AP and Reuters, put it at about 55 minutes. No joint statement or concrete agreement had been reported by midday. The Kremlin's own readout of the earlier Putin–Trump meeting lists only who attended, Marco Rubio and Scott Bessent for the US side. Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov said the two leaders discussed "the conflict in Ukraine" and that it "went well".
story.why: the warm words are the three leaders' own descriptions, and there is no sign yet of anything binding. Kyiv and European capitals, meeting separately in Berlin as a "Coalition of the Willing", fear that the three powers could settle questions about Ukraine without them. Switzerland, whose exports and sanctions policy depend on both Washington and Brussels, would be affected by any such deal.

story.headline: Israeli tanks cross Gaza's Yellow Line
story.summary: Israel launches a ground operation west of the Yellow Line in central Gaza.
story.display_body: Israeli tanks advanced west of the "Yellow Line" in central Gaza on Wednesday 18 November, the biggest ground operation since the October 2025 ceasefire. The Yellow Line marks the area Israeli forces were to pull back to under the ceasefire; Israel now controls about 60–70% of the strip. The Israeli army called it a "precise operation" to "remove a threat" to its troops. COGAT, the Israeli military body that handles civilian affairs in the Palestinian territories, told aid agencies and civilians to avoid the Bureij and Nuseirat camps and the Salah al-Din road, Gaza's main north–south route. Palestinian medics told Reuters that three people were killed in separate incidents. Hamas called the move a "flagrant violation" of the truce; Israel says it is responding to Hamas violations and rearmament. Gaza's health authorities count at least 1,600 Palestinians killed since the ceasefire took effect, and Israel reports fewer than 10 soldiers killed.
story.why: it is the clearest sign yet that the US-backed ceasefire is breaking down. A few days earlier, the "Board of Peace" that Trump set up had warned the truce was close to collapse. Most of Gaza's two million people are living through winter rains in damaged or makeshift shelter.

story.headline: Houthi missile damages Riyadh fund tower
story.summary: Houthi missile attack damages the Saudi sovereign fund tower in Riyadh.
story.display_body: A Houthi missile attack on Riyadh overnight into Thursday 19 November damaged the 80-storey tower that houses Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund, the tallest building in the city's financial district. An anonymous source told AFP that the façade was damaged over several floors and windows were blown out. The Saudi-led coalition said it had "dealt with" a missile fired at the capital and that debris fell on the city. It also said it destroyed the launch platform it says was used, at Dhamar, about 100 km south of Sanaa. The Houthis said Saudi aircraft struck a factory in Sanaa. On Tuesday 17 November, the Houthi health ministry reported that 14 civilians had been killed in coalition strikes on a factory north of Hodeida. A Houthi strike had already damaged an Aramco tower in Riyadh earlier this month.
story.why: Saudi Arabia has come under regular Houthi fire since hostilities in Yemen resumed this summer, ending the 2022 UN-brokered truce, and the Saudi financial centre is now being hit repeatedly.

story.headline: Denmark ratifies Greenland defence deal
story.summary: Danish parliament approves the US-Denmark-Greenland defence agreement.
story.display_body: Denmark's parliament approved the defence and security agreement with the United States and Greenland on Thursday 19 November, with all 109 members present voting in favour. The deal amends and supplements the 1951 agreement on the defence of Greenland. It was signed by the three governments in New York on 22 September, and Greenland's parliament, Inatsisartut, approved it earlier this month. The Folketing says Copenhagen can now formally notify Washington that both parliaments have consented, which completes ratification and makes the agreement legally binding. It allows a larger US military presence on the island while restating Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.
story.why: it formally ends a dispute that began in January, when Trump threatened force and tariffs against European allies to gain control of Greenland. Washington gets its expanded access through a treaty rather than annexation.

story.headline: Crimean Bridge hit a third time
story.summary: Third Ukrainian attack on the Crimean Bridge this week suspends rail traffic.
story.display_body: The Crimean Bridge was attacked on Thursday 19 November for the third time this week, and rail traffic was suspended, according to Sergei Aksyonov, the Russian-installed head of Crimea. Aksyonov said trains should run again from about 16:00 local time. Russia's TASS agency quoted Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin as saying some sections could take months to return to service. A Ukrainian missile and drone strike on Tuesday 17 November destroyed the steel arch over the road section of the 19-km crossing. It is the only bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea and a main supply route for Russian forces in southern Ukraine.

story.headline: Committee clears EU deal without cantons' vote
story.summary: National Council foreign affairs committee approves Bilaterals III and backs an optional referendum.
story.display_body: The National Council's foreign affairs committee (APK-N/CPE-N) approved the "stabilisation" part of the Bilaterals III package with the EU by 15 votes to 9 with 1 abstention, and voted 15 to 10 to submit it to an optional referendum, which needs only a popular majority. In its release of Wednesday 18 November, the committee rejected a mandatory referendum "sui generis", which would also need a majority of cantons. It also rejected, 16 to 8, the Council of States committee's parliamentary initiative 26.425 to approve the package at constitutional level. This puts the committee at odds with the Council of States. It also proposed implementing rules on free movement that it says use the full room for manoeuvre without breaching the agreement. That is a correction to the Council of States' autumn decisions, such as requiring EU citizens to show criminal-record extracts, which the NZZ notes conflicted with the agreement. The committee unanimously backed stronger rights for parliament to be consulted when Switzerland takes over EU law. It also voted 16 to 9 for a parliamentary office in Brussels. The bill (26.023) is now ready for the National Council's winter session.
story.why: whether the cantons also have to approve the package could decide its fate. Political scientists cited by the NZZ estimate it would need about 57% of the popular vote to be fairly sure of a majority of cantons. If the chambers still disagree after the winter session, a conciliation committee will settle it behind closed doors, and the NZZ says a single vote could decide it.

story.headline: Inquiry: 2024 Rhône flood was avoidable
story.summary: Valais parliamentary inquiry finds the 2024 Rhône flood a collective failure.
story.display_body: Valais's parliamentary inquiry into the June 2024 Rhône flood at Sierre and Chippis concluded on Thursday 19 November that the disaster was a "collective failure" of the cantonal government and administration, and probably avoidable. A flood-protection measure for this stretch, part of the Third Rhône Correction project, was put to public consultation in 2008 and never carried out. An expert opinion in the report says that if the work had been done, "it is highly likely that no overflow would have occurred" there. The inquiry found no single culprit. It describes disputes between cantonal departments that stalled the project for almost 20 years. The June 2024 flood swamped homes and the Novelis and Constellium aluminium plants and caused tens of millions of francs in damage. Some residents evacuated on the night of 29–30 June 2024 have still not returned home, and there is no timetable for the remaining work.
story.why: the Third Rhône Correction, in Valais and Vaud, is Switzerland's largest flood-protection project. It covers 162 km of river, protects about 100,000 people and is budgeted at about 3.6 billion francs. Some sections are not due before 2040, and the report says delay itself has a cost.

story.headline: Army picks Thales radar to replace TAFLIR
story.summary: armasuisse selects the Thales GM200 medium-range radar.
story.display_body: armasuisse, the federal defence procurement office, has picked Thales Suisse's French-made Ground Master 200 radar to replace the army's medium-range TAFLIR radar from the 1980s, which will be retired at the end of 2028, it said on Thursday 19 November. The semi-mobile radar detects, classifies and tracks aircraft and other targets at low, medium and high altitude. It will complement the fixed long-range FLORES radars and is meant to close gaps in Switzerland's picture of its airspace. Four European suppliers were invited to bid in April and offered five systems. Thales won mainly on the share of work going to Swiss industry and on technology transfer. This fits the Federal Council's 2025 target of placing 60% of arms purchases in Switzerland and 30% in neighbouring and other European countries. Parliament approved the purchase in the 2026 armed forces dispatch; the release gives no price.

story.headline: Commodity trading value added falls 10.8%
story.summary: Swiss commodity traders' value added dropped to 17.1 billion francs in 2025.
story.display_body: Swiss commodity-trading firms produced 17.1 billion francs of value added in 2025, 10.8% less than in 2024, the Federal Statistical Office (FSO) and the State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) said on Thursday 19 November. The offices put the fall down to high uncertainty and sharp, uneven price swings across commodities. In 2024 the sector had 1,024 firms and 11,264 jobs, and more than 90% of the jobs were in five cantons: Geneva (5,244), Zug (2,575), Ticino (1,080), Vaud (996) and Zurich (435). Fuel trading accounts for 36.4% of jobs and minerals and metals for 28.6%.
